title: How these numbers are made
intro: Every site that estimates PC performance shows you a number. This page is about the part they leave out: how the number was produced, how far off it can be, and what we do not know.

measured.heading: What is measured
measured.body: A performance index is only written for a part when there are published benchmark measurements behind it. Today that is {measuredGpu} graphics chips and {measuredCpu} processors, out of {gpuChips} chips and {cpus} processors in the catalogue. The measurements come from {points} published data points.
measured.games: Game-level FPS comes from the same measurements: {games1440} games at 1440p and {games2160} at 4K. A game enters the list only when at least three different graphics cards were measured in it.
measured.noBlend: We do not blend measurements from different reviewers. Two outlets test on different systems, drivers and scene choices; averaging them would produce a number that nobody measured.

estimated.heading: What is estimated
estimated.body: Everything else. A part without measurements gets an index predicted from its specifications, and the interface marks it with ≈ and an error band. An estimated number never pretends to be a measured one.
estimated.how: The model fits index = k × x^b inside an architecture family, where x is bus width × boost clock for graphics cards and boost clock × √L3 for processors. If a family has fewer than four measurements it cannot carry its own band, and the prediction falls back to a model trained on the other families — with that model's wider band.
estimated.cards: Add-in board cards inherit the index of their chip. A factory-overclocked card is not measured separately, and we do not invent a number for it from its clock speed.

bands.heading: What the error band means
bands.body: The band is a leave-one-out measurement, not a guess. Every measured point is predicted from the other points, without its own data, and the errors are collected. The published number is the 90th percentile: nine out of ten predictions land inside it.
bands.numbers: Game FPS: mean error {fpsMean}%, 90th percentile {fpsP90}%, worst single point {fpsMax}%. Index prediction: from ±{bandBest}% inside a well-measured family up to ±{bandWorst}% when the family has no measurements at all.
bands.worst: The worst case is published on purpose. A band that hides its tail is a marketing number.

specs.heading: Where the specifications come from
specs.body: The manufacturer's own product page is the primary source and is never overwritten. Where a manufacturer does not publish a value, an external source may fill the gap — but only into an empty field, and the source is recorded per field, not per row.
specs.wikipedia: Wikipedia currently supplies {wikiFields} values, mostly memory bandwidth and transistor counts that NVIDIA does not publish at all. Wherever such a value is displayed, the article title, revision number and CC BY-SA licence are displayed with it.
specs.checks: Stored values are checked against each other: memory bandwidth against bus width, VRAM against bus width and chip capacity, TDP against recommended power supply, and a dozen more. A value that is physically impossible is caught even when no external source disagrees. That check found and corrected an error of ours in the RTX 5060 Ti's memory bandwidth.

unknown.heading: What this site does not know
unknown.cpu: Game FPS numbers are graphics-card-limited. The processor measurements and the graphics-card measurements share no games, so the processor does not enter the FPS number at all. The interface says so where the list appears.
unknown.resolution: There are no 1080p measurements in the game list. Only 1440p and 4K.
unknown.coverage: Of {gpuCards} selectable graphics cards, only those descending from a measured chip can show game FPS. The rest show compatibility results and an estimated index.
unknown.price: Prices exist for {pricedParts} parts, entered by hand, in USD. This is not a price comparison site.
unknown.platform: Desktop only. Laptops and consoles are different hardware and are not covered.
unknown.proxy: We considered anchoring unmeasured families to public synthetic benchmark scores. The source we would have used does not permit automated access, so the idea is untested — not disproved.

audit.heading: How to check us
audit.body: Every permanent decision, including the ones that went badly, is written down with its reasoning and its date. Estimation quality is tracked against a frozen baseline, so a change that makes predictions worse fails a check rather than passing quietly.
audit.note: If a number on this site looks wrong, it is more useful to us than a compliment. The feedback box on the front page reaches the same person who wrote this page.

updated: Coverage numbers on this page are read from the database on every request, not typed into the text.
